newsitem.title: USA: Kellogg seeks OK for wheat bran anti-cancer claim.
newsitem.headline: Kellogg seeks OK for wheat bran anti-cancer claim.

text.p: Kellogg Co. plans to announce Tuesday that it is seeking permission to make a new health claim that foods with wheat bran fiber can help reduce the risk of colon cancer, officials said Monday.

The nation's largest cereal maker, battling to maintain its edge in the hotly competitive market, has asked the Food and Drug Administration to approve the claim on packages of foods containing wheat bran fiber, said Celeste Clark, Kellogg vice president of worldwide nutrition marketing.

Kellogg, based in Battle Creek, Mich., has about 15 food products that contain wheat bran fiber, including the top-selling cereals Kellogg's Raisin Bran, Frosted Mini-Wheats, All-Bran and Complete Bran Flakes.

Clark said the petition is backed up by 100 different studies spanning 25 years that show that dietary fiber from wheat bran, when included in a low-fat, high-fiber diet, can reduce colon cancer risk.
"I think it's important to point out that this would be applicable to a wide range of foods not exclusive to Kellogg, including whole wheat breads and crackers," she said.
In January, Kellogg rival Quaker Oats Co. won final approval to make the claim that foods containing soluble fiber from whole oats, when eaten in a low-fat, high-fiber diet, can reduce cholesterol.

The approval, which gave a boost to Quaker's best selling cereals, ended a two-year process for the Chicago-based food conglomerate. Clark declined to say how long Kellogg expected the FDA to consider the company's petition.

Kellogg is already awaiting an FDA decision on a petition filed filed last June to claim that soluble fiber in foods containing psyllium, a type of grain, also reduces cholesterol. Kellogg currently sells a cereal called Bran Buds With psyllium.
FDA approval of the wheat bran fiber claim would mark the first time the agency has allowed a food-specific health claim for insoluble fiber.
FDA now allows companies to make the general claim that a diet low in fat and high in fiber from fruits, vegetables and grains helps reduce the risk of certain types of cancers.
Clark said the Kellogg petition will show that wheat bran fiber helps to dilute potential carcinogens in the colon and reduce the time it takes for feces to move through the bowel.
She said the National Cancer Institute recommends that Americans eat 25 to 30 grams of dietary fiber a day but that most people eat only 11 to 15 grams a day.
